  4. We buy your pods (the follicles that hold the seeds and floss) every fall, either picked by you or harvested mechanically by Lasclay.

A clip made from what we already had.

The body is recycled clear PETG. We did not buy this plastic: it comes from our own production tooling, made redundant when the way we manufacture changed. Ground, remelted and moulded by Unique Plastique, in Québec City, it becomes an object you use every day.

Two versions. The clear one is the plastic alone, transparent, just as it comes out of our tooling. The brown one contains milkweed seed cake, what is left after the oil is pressed. That is what gives it its black-flecked amber, with no added pigment, and no two brown clips are alike.

To be clear: in the brown version, milkweed does not insulate anything and plays no technical role. It adds colour, and above all it gives a use to a residue that would otherwise serve no purpose. The clear version contains no milkweed at all.

Milkweed seed planting guide

We put together a simplified guide to sum up the essentials. The method for planting milkweed seeds depends on the season. You can of course keep your seeds until the season that suits you best.

Planting in the fall (October/November)

Planting in the fall is simpler, but the germination rate may be lower.

Planting

Ideally, use well-drained, fairly light or sandy soil in a spot that gets enough sun. Keep in mind that it is important to plant before the ground freezes.

Planting in the spring (May/June)

To plant in the spring, the seeds must be stratified first.

Stratification

In a sealed plastic bag (Ziploc type), mix the seeds with damp sand or perlite. Preferably use distilled or dechlorinated water (tap water left out in the open for 24 hours) and squeeze as much air as possible out of the bag.

Place the sealed bag in the refrigerator at 5°C for at least 30 days.


Seed bomb planting guide

Planting period: May to early August

Step 1 - Planning

Find and assess the spot where you want your seed bombs to germinate. Depending on the species you chose, it is essential to pick the right location (soil, sunlight, etc.) before planting. To help, information sheets are available on the product pages for the milkweed bombs, while the native flower bombs come in themes that guide gardeners (e.g. "Wetlands" flower bombs).

Step 2 - Planting

Drop the bomb where you want it and cover it lightly with potting soil so that birds, rodents or the weather don't get to the seeds. Space them about 30 cm apart and set them no deeper than 5 mm.

We recommend not planting the bombs before May, to reduce the risk of a late overnight frost as much as possible. Depending on your region, the ideal planting period runs from May 1 to August 1. In the fall, it is better to plant untreated (non-cold-stratified) seeds directly in the ground.

Step 3 - Watering

Water lightly when planting and keep the soil moist during germination. Be careful not to soak the soil. It is important not to water every day, as this can rot the seeds and stop them from germinating. Once the plants are up, they no longer need watering: rainfall is enough for them to grow well.

In dry spells and heat waves, you can water up to twice a week as needed.

For seeds planted in pots, water once or twice a week or as needed.

Frequently asked questions

Where should I plant my seed bombs?

It depends on which type of bomb you have and the seeds it contains. All the botanical information is on our website, on the product pages for the bombs: soil type, sunlight, plant type, etc. For the milkweed bombs, since each bomb contains a single species, we were able to print basic botanical information right on the packets.

How can I improve the yield and long-term establishment of the bombs?

In terms of preparation, we have already done what is needed to encourage germination. That said, a good way to ensure the plants' long-term success is to weed a radius of at least 6 inches, ideally 12 inches, around the spot where each cell will be planted, to limit competition from other perennials.

Can unused bombs be kept for later?

Yes, by putting them back in the refrigerator as soon as you receive them. Doing so, however, carries a real risk of greatly reducing future germination. Here's why: during shipping, the bombs return to room temperature for a few days, which can signal the seeds to come out of their cold dormancy and start germinating. Putting them back in the fridge may send the seeds that hadn't germinated yet back into dormancy, but those that had started to germinate will probably die.

Is it normal for my bombs to show mould on the surface?
Yes, completely! Our seed bomb mix contains mycorrhizal spores, beneficial fungi that germinate and help plants draw nutrients from deeper in the soil.

Common milkweed (Asclepias syriaca), sometimes called American silk, is a plant native to North America that colonizes unused fields, vacant lots and even roadsides.

Nature lovers and even beginners recognize it easily. Whether in bloom, with its almost perfectly spherical flower umbels, or when its pods split open to release seeds and white floss, milkweed catches the eye of anyone passing by.

Common milkweed is the best-known and most widespread species of the subfamily Asclepiadoideae, itself part of the dogbane family (Apocynaceae), which includes more than 2,000 species. Common milkweed's natural range runs from Québec to Texas, north to south, and from Oregon to Nova Scotia, west to east. It is the species grown commercially in Canada for its white floss: insulating, water-repellent, rot-resistant, hypoallergenic, antibacterial and absorbent.

In Québec and Eastern Canada, four milkweed species are native:

  • Common milkweed (Asclepias syriaca), with pink flowers
  • Swamp milkweed (Asclepias incarnata), with mauve flowers
  • Butterfly milkweed (Asclepias tuberosa), with orange flowers
  • Poke milkweed (Asclepias exaltata), with white flowers

A gold mine for pollinators

The abundance and diversity of insects that visit milkweed is no accident:

  • It overflows with sugar-rich nectar (3%).
  • Its pollen is also renewed over the life of the flower, which is unusual.
  • Its blooming period is also unusually long compared with other plants, about 4 weeks for a colony.

A few of the many pollinators that visit milkweed flowers.


Host plant of the monarch butterfly

Milkweed is the exclusive host plant of the monarch butterfly (Danaus plexippus). Their symbiotic relationship goes back millions of years and is so complex that science has yet to unravel all of its mysteries.

  1. Milkweed sap naturally contains substances called cardenolides, which are toxic to most animals, including many of the monarch's predators and parasites.

  2. Female monarchs lay their eggs exclusively on milkweed plants spread along their migration route, from Mexico to Canada.

  3. The caterpillars feed on milkweed leaves to self-medicate against parasites and to become toxic to many of their potential predators.

  4. The caterpillars form their chrysalis near the milkweed plant they were born on, where a butterfly emerges that will feed on milkweed nectar, among others (helping pollination), as well as other flowers depending on the time of summer it emerges.



What sets the monarch apart is that instead of breaking down or excreting the toxins in its food, as many animals with similar behaviour do, the monarch larva accumulates them in its tissues and keeps them even after it transforms into a butterfly. The concentration of cardenolides in a monarch caterpillar or butterfly is therefore much higher than in a milkweed plant, making them effectively toxic to many predators and parasites. A few other specialist insects (milkweed bugs, the milkweed longhorn beetle, the milkweed leaf beetle, the milkweed aphid, etc.) have developed the same evolutionary strategy, sporting the same colours as the monarch.

Since the relationship is symbiotic, milkweed also shows signs of co-evolution with the monarch and other herbivores. The plant seems to heal faster and faster from attacks by its herbivorous predators, the monarch caterpillar among them. Its reproduction also depends in part on pollination by adult monarchs feeding on the abundant nectar of its flowers.

It becomes almost impossible to describe the monarch without mentioning milkweed, and vice versa.

Milkweed floss as a high-performance thermal insulation

The fibres attached to milkweed seeds are what we commonly call milkweed floss, American silk or Québec silk. These hollow fibres, shaped like almost perfectly round micro-tubes, trap air and create a thermal, acoustic and water-resistant barrier that is surprising for a plant material. When milkweed floss is used as a filling or laid out as an insulating textile membrane, the air held inside the fibres (the lumen) adds to the layers of air trapped between the fibres. This unique property creates an ideal barrier against heat transfer, making it possible to build outdoor accessories that are thin, light, and whose thermal insulation holds its own against synthetic or animal-based materials.

Another interesting property makes the fibres even better suited as a lining for outdoor clothing: they are naturally coated with a wax that makes them hydrophobic, meaning they repel water. So on top of keeping you warm, milkweed-insulated clothing keeps you dry! That is an impressive advantage over the other textile insulations on the market, such as down, polyester or wool, which soak up water easily and hold on to moisture, while having a much heavier ecological and ethical footprint.

And the advantage is twofold: milkweed repels moisture from the outside (snow, rain, etc.) as much as from the inside (sweat).

Other industrial uses

Flotation material
A bit of history: during the Second World War, when the supply of kapok from Asia was cut off by Japan, milkweed was harvested on a large scale in Canada and the United States to produce a textile fibre used to fill the life vests of sailors and airmen. Thanks to its hydrophobic properties, milkweed floats for up to 8 hours straight. All of this was before synthetic materials came along, of course. Unfortunately, this potential has since been abandoned.


Oil spill absorbent
The same goes for milkweed's many other economic uses. One of the most promising today is without a doubt as a high-performance absorbent for oil spills. The same tubular fibre structure that gives it its insulating property also makes it lipophilic, meaning it can hold oily substances. It goes without saying that this characteristic would be very useful for containing petroleum spills in aquatic environments. Weight for weight, milkweed absorbs 5 times more diesel than the material most commonly used for this purpose today (polypropylene), while floating perfectly and absorbing no water at all! Milkweed is a remarkable alternative here, especially when you consider the irony of today's oil absorbent industry, whose products are made from... oil!

Bedding fill
An American company, Ogallala, uses milkweed blended with down as the fill for its bedding and pillows. Naturally hypoallergenic, milkweed repels moisture, dust and dust mites. It gives Ogallala's products an edge over the competition, and its users a better night's sleep than everyone around them!

Cosmetics
The oil extracted from milkweed seeds is being closely studied for its potential as a base for cosmetics such as skin lotions or sunscreen. Through a chemical process, it is possible to turn the triglycerides in milkweed oil into compounds that absorb UV rays. Perhaps a little further off, but very promising all the same!

The milkweed revolution is here, all around us... all that's left is to harvest it!

Milkweed coats and the offshoring compromise
Milkweed coats, offshoring and the environmental compromise
Lasclay explains candidly the offshoring compromise behind its milkweed-insulated coats: costs, accessibility and environmental impact.

When are the Lasclay coats coming?

Since our very beginnings, dozens of times a week, this question keeps coming back.

Every time, we gave the same answers:

"Maybe someday, but not right away!"
"We're focusing on small accessories to introduce the powers of milkweed to as many people as possible. The merino wool sock strategy, basically!"

Well, our answer has now changed. More than a year ago, we started developing a first milkweed coat and a sleeveless vest, products that are truly one of a kind.

When we say first, we mean for us... Because there have been milkweed coats on the market before. Did they give milkweed a good reputation?

Yes... and no.

Very warm and light, like most products insulated with this fibre, they were appreciated by the people who wore them, but they never managed to break into the market. Whether it was the $1,000 Quartz parkas or the $500-plus Atypic puffer jackets, few units were sold, both products were discontinued, and in the end some great opportunities to put milkweed on the map were lost. A series of decisions, logical or not, stuck a label on this material. People ended up thinking, "Well, milkweed, I'll never know if it's warm, it's too expensive, it's a luxury product."

We have always said it: a plant that grows in sidewalk cracks in the middle of downtown, and that is so abundant, should not be marketed as an overpriced product whose scarcity is kept up artificially. We need to develop it, industrialize it responsibly and democratize it. It is a collective resource that everyone should have access to.

But how do we get there, given the dead end at the heart of the great social project that milkweed represents in Québec?

Because yes, there is a kind of dead end, a paradox in the development of the milkweed industry, and in all honesty, it may be what made the milkweed coats of the past so expensive.

On one side, we have a material grown in Québec with strong industrial and environmental potential, but which is brand new and not very developed technologically. We process it in Québec, we introduce it to people while learning to tame it, but to do that, we have little choice but to start by doing everything locally and making small, minimalist accessories, to keep prices as affordable as possible and build momentum.


On the other side, the textile industry has been offshored for 40 years and is in very poor shape in North America. Contrary to popular belief, it is not just a matter of wage differences: expertise and skilled labour have become rare here, and some specialized machines no longer exist here, or never did. A lot has happened in 40 years, and global textile production is now far ahead of us: robots, connected factories, the internet, and so on!

So those who tried to produce a milkweed coat in the past were faced with two options, each as unpleasant as the other:

1. Ship milkweed to the other side of the world so it can come back here (the main market) as finished products: complete commercial and environmental nonsense.


2. Make a technical, complex and labour-intensive product locally under the conditions listed above, causing costs to explode and limiting the options for the product's finish quality.

Our predecessors chose the second option, with the results mentioned above...

But are those really the only choices? Or, with a little creativity, could we find a middle ground?
That is the question we asked ourselves, and it led to a leap forward as unexpected as it is ingenious.

What if we did each step of a milkweed coat in the best possible place, wherever that may be? If sewing costs too much in Québec for a product like this, could we do it elsewhere and keep everything to do with milkweed here?

After all, the greatest benefit of Québec's milkweed industry is without question keeping the fields in production, fields that support so much biodiversity, including threatened monarch butterflies. We firmly believe this, and honestly think this mission justifies a few compromises.

A revolutionary idea was born: a coat with removable insulating pads made in Québec, inserted into a shell pre-assembled elsewhere in the world, where the expertise and technology are. These removable milkweed pads, a bit like our fisherman beanie, adapt to the changing temperatures of the four seasons: you put the milkweed in for the freezing temperatures of winter, and take some or all of it out when spring arrives and the weather is milder!

The concept also makes the coat more durable (you can replace only the insulation if it wears out after a few years) and breaks the commercial deadlock that sank past milkweed coat projects (see below).

Our removable insulation concept gets milkweed out of this dead end: we keep the production of milkweed insulation, for which we have developed unique expertise, here at home, and we sustain the milkweed crops that are so beneficial for the environment. We amplify this positive impact by making elsewhere the parts that are impossible to make here, where we are not competitive.

For more details on this project, here is a short video that explains it further. I produced it as part of the Première Ovation Design grant, which I received personally to develop this project.

Why is this pre-sale crucial for the future of Lasclay and of milkweed?

This pre-sale is much more than a chance to get coats at a reduced price. It is literally essential to the future of Lasclay and of milkweed in Québec.

Developing bigger, more complex products like coats, sleeping bags or bedding, which use more milkweed than our small accessories, is crucial to keeping milkweed in cultivation. We are at a critical point.
Of the 125 milkweed growers who got started in Québec between 2014 and 2018, only 20 remain. They need income, hope and market outlets to keep growing this crop, which has become a lifeline for endangered monarch butterflies.

Lasclay's milkweed coat is therefore a decisive project : if it succeeds, it will help make milkweed farming and our company profitable, and it will open the way to a host of other milkweed products, ones that are highly interesting and in demand. With your contribution and your trust, we can get this wheel turning and clear the path toward a bright future for milkweed in Québec, making it a true flagship industry, which has been our ambition since day one.

This beautiful plant deserves it. The monarch butterflies deserve it. The courageous milkweed growers deserve it. And you, our loyal community who have supported us from the start, you finally deserve the products you have been asking us for, for so long.

Yet at the turn of the 2010s, a handful of Quebecers bet that it could become an industry. What followed was a genuine roller coaster: outsized promises, a brutal collapse, and a struggle that continues today. And this saga is inseparable from that of the monarch butterfly.

The beginnings: from a hemp field to an industry

It all starts with an astonishing fibre. When the milkweed pod opens in the fall, it releases a light, white floss, long known as American silk. Each filament is a tiny hollow tube coated in wax: weight for weight, the air it traps makes it an insulation that rivals down, while being naturally water-repellent, hypoallergenic and even a good acoustic insulator. As early as the late 1980s, Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada had shown that its yield per hectare could match that of cotton.

The modern adventure, though, began almost by chance. In Sainte-Thècle, in the Mauricie region, farmer Daniel Allard of Ferme Algo was growing hemp when he crossed paths with textile specialists fascinated by milkweed. One of them, engineer François Simard of the company Encore3, passed on what he knew. The plant's floss had been known for a long time, but almost everything about growing it as a field crop remained to be invented. In the spring of 2012, the small Québec group flew to Illinois to meet Dr. Winthrop Phippen, a leading authority on milkweed as a crop, then launched a first trial with the support of Québec's agriculture ministry (MAPAQ): 115,000 seedlings started in greenhouses, transplanted onto half a hectare, and immediately visited by monarch caterpillars. The plants held up. Proof of concept.

2013-2014: an industry takes shape

A new industry was born. Daniel Allard founded the Coopérative Monark to support growers (seed, harvesting equipment, fibre processing) and offer them purchase contracts of 10 hectares each. The ambition was clear: reach 1,000 hectares under cultivation to guarantee a steady supply, a collective project valued at $1.1 million. By the fall of 2013, the first seven growers had signed on; in 2014, about 300 hectares were in the ground, in Mauricie, the Bas-Saint-Laurent, the Eastern Townships and the Outaouais. In parallel, Encore3 developed its own machines to extract the fibre from the pods.

The targeted markets were many: spinning, coat insulation, oil absorbents, insulation panels, hypoallergenic bedding. Protec-Style won a contract with Parks Canada for emergency spill kits distributed in 54 national parks, then a contract with the Canadian Coast Guard for milkweed-insulated liners, vests, gloves and mittens, two promising milestones that would nonetheless be lost later on.

The crux of the matter: harvesting milkweed

Behind the enthusiasm lay a stubborn problem: harvesting milkweed by machine. No existing equipment could do it, and the window is tiny, barely two weeks between the moment the pods ripen and the moment they release their seeds to the wind. These damp, fragile pods then have to be dried quickly, and the very delicate fibre breaks, producing a lot of dust. Designing a suitable harvester quickly became the industry's central challenge. Two ambitious machine projects took it on, and both failed; in the opinion of several people we spoke with, these setbacks were mainly due to poorly managed development projects entrusted to underqualified people.

For lack of anything better, milkweed was long harvested by hand. Two approaches eventually emerged, and they need to be told apart. The first, semi-mechanized, relies on a simple comb mounted on a tractor, which already makes it possible to harvest some 2,000 kg per day. The second, far more advanced, is a dedicated harvester developed by an independent grower, at least five times more productive. This missing piece, reliable mechanized harvesting, has been cited again and again as the reason the industry failed to get off the ground. We detail this technical saga in our article on harvesting milkweed.

Milkweed fibre, too warm for Everest

Even before it reached store shelves, American silk was about to face a spectacular test. In 2016, Québec mountaineer Jean-François Tardif set off for Everest dressed in milkweed-insulated prototypes: a light anorak, a one-piece suit and a blanket, cut from an orange fibre that deliberately recalled the monarch's wings. For health reasons, he would not reach the summit. But at high altitude, his verdict was unequivocal: he found his clothing warm enough, even too warm for the Himalayas, in temperatures ranging from -22 to +25 degrees in the sun. Weight for weight, the fibre rivalled down, while being water-repellent and less bulky. The roadside weed had just proven, on the roof of the world, that it could keep a person warm in the most extreme conditions.

2016: the coat that changed everything

In October 2016, the manufacturer Quartz Co. launched, with Altitude Sports, a first winter coat insulated with milkweed, in a limited edition, at around $800. The image was striking: the roadside weed, the one that grows in sidewalk cracks, sewn into a high-end parka worn in the city. It was a kind of consecration. But it was also, though no one saw it yet, the seed of a misunderstanding. At that price and in such small quantities, selling at best a few hundred units, a coat like this could never generate the volume the crop desperately needed to become profitable. Other products, launched later, would contain only a tiny share of milkweed, offering almost no support to growers. Little by little, a false idea took hold: milkweed was a luxury product.

2017-2018: the collapse

Then everything fell apart. In October 2017, Protec-Style and its subsidiaries Les Industries Encore3 and Fibre Monark declared bankruptcy, with liabilities of more than $1.4 million. Encore3 alone had reserved nearly 90% of the harvest under way; the growers, who had invested nearly $2 million to prepare their land, were left without a buyer. Quartz Co., cut off from its supply, produced its coats for only two seasons and ended the line in 2018. Discouraged, many growers gave up the crop in turn.

How did it come to this? The causes pile up. The first, as we have seen, was the lack of reliable mechanized harvesting, which deprived processors of sufficient volume and consistent quality. The second was an ambition too broad, too fast: Protec-Style was trying to break through on several fronts at once, from oil absorbents to membranes and insulation, which one of its own people would later sum up as "a mistake to want to move too fast in every area". On top of that came debts that grew too heavy, particularly around the harvester project, until they drained the company's supply and its finances.

A loss for Québec and for the monarch

It is worth measuring what was at stake. This was not just a company going bankrupt: it was an emerging economic flagship, a source of jobs, know-how and pride, that was weakened and remains precarious today. Québec had an industry that was nearly unique in the world, and it very nearly let it slip away.

For the monarch, the setback is crueller still. Its caterpillar eats only one plant: milkweed. And its population in Mexico, in free fall since the 1990s, had started climbing again around 2013-2014, at the very moment the crop was getting started in Québec and Vermont.

Correlation is not causation, and we say so plainly. But a University of Guelph study published in the Journal of Animal Ecology points precisely to the loss of breeding habitat, in other words the decline of milkweed (about 21% between 1995 and 2013), as the driver of the monarch's decline. The industry had, almost without meaning to, grown vast fields of milkweed, each one a refuge for the butterfly. When those fields were cleared for other crops, a large share of that habitat, on the order of 80%, vanished along with the industry. The economic bet and the fate of the monarch were, and remain, inextricably linked. To understand this link in depth, read our page on the monarch butterfly.

Our place in this story

It is precisely this urgency that drives us forward. Where the industry stumbled, for lack of markets and because of a fragmentation in which everyone worked in isolation on their own link of the chain, we chose to act, and to act fast.

When we started out in 2020, we made a bet that went against the grain: instead of a luxury coat, start small, with mittens. A lean, self-reliant launch, designed to break into the market quickly and prove milkweed's potential to as many people as possible. Since then, we have embraced a deliberately aggressive, and risky, approach: invest, dare, and broaden the range, from mittens all the way to milkweed-insulated soft coolers, where others pulled back. And it is paying off. What sets us apart cannot be outsourced: a real, slightly obsessive love for the plant; multidisciplinary know-how that takes us through every step of its chain; and the will to maximize the share of milkweed in our products rather than dilute it, because that is what gives growers breathing room.

Everything we do flows from one conviction: what will save milkweed and its cultivation is volume. A plant this abundant should not end up as an overpriced product; it must be democratized, even if that means making the compromises that make it possible, because an accessible product sold in large numbers supports infinitely more fields than an exceptional object sold in a few hundred units. That is why we turn the old model upside down: not an $800 parka, but a coat under $300, designed around a simple, novel idea: removable milkweed insulation. Pads you insert in winter and take out in the warm season, which make the coat useful year-round, more durable, and finally commercially viable, where previous projects had bogged down.

By turning milkweed floss into useful, desirable products, we give people an economic reason to plant those fields again, and therefore to recreate monarch habitat. The product is the means; the mission is the end. Our ambition is anything but modest: to make milkweed a true world-class flagship rooted in Québec, and a concrete engine for saving the monarch. And if you want to do something with your own hands, it also starts in your backyard, with a few milkweed seeds.

A much older story than you'd think

This restart in the 2010s is only the latest chapter in a very long story. Back in the 18th century, milkweed was already called "American silk," and it is said that Louis XV wore garments trimmed with its fibre, before its use fell away after the Conquest. And during the Second World War, when the supply of kapok was cut off, schoolchildren harvested milkweed pods to fill soldiers' life vests. These chapters are now part of the same series, ready to read today.

From weed to the hope of a threatened species, milkweed has never stopped making itself useful. It is a story that deserves to be continued.

A plant with a thousand uses

Long before the French arrived, the Indigenous peoples of North America already knew milkweed and used nearly every part of it. In the St. Lawrence Valley, the Wendat made cordage from it and material for clothing, and they were the ones who taught the first French settlers to boil the young pods, otherwise toxic, to eat them. Elsewhere, the fibre of the stems, harvested in the fall once the plant had dried, yielded the same sturdy cordage: the Menominee made rope, sewing thread and fishing line from it, the Meskwaki thread, and the Cherokee bowstrings.

At the table, the plant demanded caution, since raw it is toxic. Boiled, however, its young shoots, flower buds and young pods fed many nations. The Haudenosaunee ate them in spring, the Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) used them to thicken soups, "like okra," the Meskwaki dried them for winter, and the Omaha, Pawnee and Ponca of the Missouri Valley prepared them like asparagus.

The pharmacopoeia was not left out. The plant's white latex was used to remove warts, by the Cherokee as well as the Haudenosaunee, who also applied it to stings and cuts. Closer to home, in the St. Lawrence Valley, botanist Jacques Rousseau recorded in 1945 the uses of the Kanien'kehá:ka of Kahnawà:ke: the floss of the pods as a poultice on ailing parts of the body, and a root infusion used by women.

All of this knowledge concerns the plant. Further south, it is through the butterfly that people know it. In the highlands of central Mexico, where monarchs spend the winter clustered on oyamel firs, the Purépecha and Mazahua see in their return, around the Day of the Dead, the souls of the departed coming back for a night. The link between milkweed and the monarch, though, is woven further north, on the breeding grounds where the caterpillar feeds on nothing else.

"Of Syria": the story of a mix-up

For a long time, milkweed carried a traveller's name without ever having travelled. In 1635, the Parisian physician and botanist Jacques-Philippe Cornut illustrated and described it in his Canadensium Plantarum aliarumque nondum editarum Historia, considered the very first botanical treatise devoted to the flora of North America. A delicious detail: Cornut never set foot in America. He worked from plants brought back from Canada and grown in the Parisian gardens of the Robin and Morin families. BAnQ, Québec's national library, also notes that he was not the first to report this "plant with silky fibres": Jacques Cartier and Marc Lescarbot had mentioned it before him, in vaguer terms.

The trouble is that Cornut thought he recognized in this Canadian plant a dogbane from the Levant that had already been described, and saddled it with the epithet "syriacum." A century later, in 1753, Linnaeus repeated the error without correcting it and carved it into the Latin name for good: Asclepias syriaca, "milkweed of Syria." The plant is North American through and through, but the mix-up has stuck to it ever since. As for the French name "soyer," it came later, from naturalist Charles-Sigisbert Sonnini de Manoncourt, who introduced it to France as a textile plant and devoted an entire treatise to it around 1810. From "syriaca" to "soyer," the plant has never stopped causing confusion.

A "froth like cotton"

The French settlers soon took an interest. In 1640, the governor of New France, Charles Huault de Montmagny, sent the Ursulines of Québec a "certain froth that is like cotton," with an instruction reported by Marie de l'Incarnation: beat it or card it "to see whether it could be spun," because it was "finer than silk and than beaver." In all likelihood, this was milkweed floss, already being put to the question that has followed it ever since: can it be spun? In 1640, as for a long time afterward, the answer was disappointing.

American silk, the European fashion

In the 18th century, Europe fell for this light, lustrous plant wadding. According to the Bibliothèque nationale de France, stockings and gloves were made from it in Naples, along with fabrics that required little suppleness; elsewhere, the floss filled cushions, comforters and hats, as a substitute for down and feathers. On paper, the dream was superb: a silk that grows by the roadside, free and abundant.

Reality pushed back. Milkweed fibre is short, smooth and hollow, and the very qualities that make it so warm make it almost impossible to spin on its own: it slips, it does not catch. To get a strong thread from it, it has to be blended with cotton or wool, and the result often falls short of the promises. Three centuries before our workshops, the same tension was already there: a marvellous material, and terribly hard to tame.

Rouvière, the king's hosier

The great French promoter of American silk was a Parisian hosier, Jacques de la Rouvière, who made the wardrobe of Louis XV. Won over by this fibre from Canada, he obtained a formal privilege from the king: a decree of the Council of State, signed at Versailles on October 4, 1757, authorized him to make and sell fabrics from "a material he discovered, called houette or thistle." He even devoted an essay to it in 1770, and the naturalist Sonnini an entire treatise in 1810. It is said that Louis XV himself wore it, though no contemporary source confirms this.

The venture, however, may have turned sour. Around 1760, Rouvière is said to have launched a fabric called "la soyeuse," before finding himself, according to the Bibliothèque nationale de France, in court: his cloth allegedly contained not a shred of milkweed. The fibre, too short and too smooth to spin on its own, would have been blended with something else, or replaced outright. With no archive to pin it down, the episode remains hearsay, passed from one compilation to the next.

It nonetheless has a familiar ring. Three centuries later, the temptation is the same: sell the prestige of milkweed while slipping only a pinch of it into the product, just enough to print the word on the label. Rouvière's "soyeuse" may not have contained a single strand; some pieces sold today contain little more than a handful. The plant, for its part, has never rewarded those who coveted its name without its substance.

Forgotten after the Conquest

Then the thread snapped. After the British Conquest of 1760, the Empire was awash in cheap silk and cotton; milkweed, finicky to spin and costly to process, fell back to the rank of weed. Its cultivation was abandoned, its uses forgotten. For nearly two centuries, without anyone paying attention, the plant would serve only to feed the caterpillars of the monarch butterfly, which lays its eggs on nothing else. It is a curious legacy: the weed that humans abandoned quietly became the cradle of one of the continent's greatest travellers.

A thread that never really broke

What this story reminds us is that milkweed was never just a weed. Three centuries before our mittens, it was already clothing people, already healing, already intriguing, and already resisting those who wanted to tame it. At Lasclay, we are picking up this old thread with new tools and the same conviction: this plant deserves better than oblivion, and better than a mere name on a label. This time, its return also benefits the monarch butterfly, which never let go of it.

Milkweed and the Second World War | Lasclay
Cut off from kapok, the Allies filled their life vests with milkweed floss, harvested by schoolchildren. The forgotten story.

In the fall of 1944, the fate of thousands of sailors rested, in part, on a weed that children were gathering along ditches, in onion sacks. Far from the din of battle, a silent army of schoolchildren, scouts and 4-H club members combed the fields of some thirty American states and Canada, picking milkweed pods. Their harvest would float under the arms of the crews of the U.S. Navy. Here is how a plant despised by farmers became, for the length of a war, an unlikely hero.

When the kapok ran out

Before the war, the U.S. Navy's life vests slept full of kapok, a light, buoyant fibre taken from a tropical tree and grown almost exclusively in Southeast Asia, mainly on Java, in the Dutch East Indies, today's Indonesia. The supply seemed eternal. It collapsed in a single season. In early 1942, the Japanese advance on Java abruptly closed the kapok route to American ports. Overnight, the world's foremost navy found itself without the fibre that kept its men on the surface, at the very moment the war was spreading across two oceans.

A replacement was needed, and it was needed yesterday. In their laboratories, Navy engineers tested dozens of buoyant materials one by one: plant fibres, foams, corks. Nearly all of them failed: too heavy, too fragile, quickly waterlogged with salt water. Then an unlikely candidate stood out, a plant no one would have thought of cultivating, the one that grew on its own in the ditches and fallow fields of North America: milkweed.

A fibre that floats

Milkweed's secret lies in the structure of its floss. Each filament is a fine hollow tube whose wall is coated with a thin layer of natural wax. The tube traps air, the wax repels water, and the whole floats with remarkable stubbornness. According to Navy tests, a single pound of this floss kept a 150-pound man afloat. The fibre proved as warm as wool but far lighter, and more buoyant than cork. On paper, it was the ideal solution.

There remained the obstacle that would complicate everything: hundreds of tons of it had to be produced, without time to cultivate a single hectare. Milkweed floss is not harvested like cotton, in orderly fields. It lay dormant in millions of pods scattered at random across the landscape, and no supply chain existed to process it. A Chicago physician would take on this problem with the tenacity of a missionary.

Boris Berkman, the man of a single plant

Dr. Boris Berkman was a physician and inventor in Chicago, and he believed in milkweed the way one believes in a cause. Well before the war, he had convinced himself that this scorned plant held an exceptional fibre, and as early as 1939 he had filed a patent for a "milkweed gin," a machine designed to separate the floss from the seeds. Over his lifetime, he accumulated more than twenty milkweed-related patents, from factory processes to the most unexpected ideas, ear muffs or coat linings.

When the kapok ran out, his hour had come. In March 1942, he brought his fibre before the House agriculture committee, badgered the Navy and won the right to put it to the test. The trials proved him right. The Navy announced it wanted a million pounds of floss, a figure so dizzying that, as one newspaper of the day admitted, "nobody believed it." Berkman believed it enough to found the Milkweed Floss Corporation of America and take its helm. The war was finally giving his plant the stage it had been waiting for.

"Two bags save one life"

Growing milkweed in time was out of reach. So the wild plant would be harvested. Starting in 1943, and above all in the fall of 1944, a huge national campaign enlisted some thirty states east of the Rockies and Canada. The men were at the front, the women in the factories; that left the children. Schoolchildren, Boy Scouts, Girl Scouts and 4-H clubs set out, bags in hand, behind a slogan of fearsome efficiency: "Two bags save one life." Never had a phrase said so simply that an armful of pods could be worth a man's life.

The deal was clear. Pickers were handed mesh onion sacks, and the government paid fifteen cents per full sack, five more if the pods were well dried. A sack held six to eight hundred pods; two were needed for a single vest. The instructions left no room for approximation: pick the ripe, browning pods while still closed, before the wind carried off the floss; never gather them wet. The mesh of the sack had its purpose: to let air through. The harvest was then hung astride fences, in the sun and wind, during the day, so the floss would dry without moulding.

Petoskey, milkweed capital of the world

All of this harvest converged on a single point on the globe: the small town of Petoskey, in northern Michigan, chosen because the shores of Lake Michigan were overrun with milkweed and a port and a railway conveniently met there. Contrary to a persistent legend, the plant did not set up in a sawmill, but in the requisitioned premises of a large local lumber and building supply company, Preston Feather & Sons, handed over to the Milkweed Floss Corporation of America.

Inside, the ingenuity bordered on inspired tinkering. A large kiln swallowed pods from every corner of the country, since other states also shipped their harvest to Petoskey. Then seven gins, the famous milkweed gins patented by Berkman, gently crushed the pods to release the floss, which was separated from the seeds and husks, baled, and shipped to the vest manufacturers. For the length of a war, a small Michigan town reigned as the milkweed capital of the world, a crown as improbable as it was short-lived.

The USS Indianapolis and the share of uncertainty

History has kept a chilling scene. On July 30, 1945, the cruiser USS Indianapolis, which had just delivered components of the first atomic bomb to Tinian, was ripped open by torpedoes from a Japanese submarine and sank in twelve minutes. Nearly nine hundred men survived the sinking, then drifted for days in the Pacific, without enough rafts, at the mercy of thirst, sun and sharks. For many, between life and the abyss, there was only the fabric of a life vest.

Were those vests filled with milkweed floss from Petoskey? Several survivors have said so, as has the Petoskey museum. A Wisconsin volunteer, Beverly Walker, who had picked the plant as a child, met former Indianapolis sailors decades later at a reunion; several told her the fibre in their vests had kept them alive. The Navy was indeed filling its vests with this floss at the time, which makes the account credible, even if no archive allows it to be confirmed vest by vest.

What milkweed really delivered

The figures of this epic grow with the years, and it is better to separate two things: the pods picked and the floss actually obtained. On the harvest side, several million pounds of pods gathered by children across the country are often cited, sometimes far more. The floss produced, though, was more modest. According to the Navy's 1946 report, barely 88,000 pounds of floss came off the lines in 1943, and the program, closed in August 1945, totalled only about 1.6 million pounds over three years, far from the five million hoped for in 1945 alone.

The same report does not hide the material's limits. Gathered in the wild, under uneven conditions, the floss offered variable quality and not always the buoyancy promised by the first tests. It mostly filled ordinary vests, sometimes disposable ones, cut for amphibious landings. Then the war ended, and the necessity with it. Asian kapok returned, fibreglass took over, and the 1945 harvest stayed in the fields, with no takers. The Petoskey plant went dark. Berkman fought on to make milkweed a peacetime crop, for clothing or latex, without ever recovering the momentum of the war. His plant returned to the oblivion of the ditches, its army of children sent back to school.

A plant that has already proven itself

There is something striking in remembering that this weed has already, in the midst of turmoil, helped keep men alive. The same hollow, water-repellent fibre that floated in the vests of 1944 warms mittens and coats today. At Lasclay, we read in it a quiet promise: milkweed is only waiting for a good reason to come back, and the war had given it one, brutal and fleeting. This time, the stakes are gentler: recreating the habitat of the monarch butterfly, which depends entirely on it to be reborn each spring.

Harvesting milkweed has made and unmade the industry: a two-week window, failed prototypes, a mechanized comb and a dedicated harvester. The technical side of the milkweed story.

Harvesting milkweed is closer to engineering than to farming. The difficulty comes from the plant itself, whose entire biology is geared toward scattering its floss to the wind at the precise moment it would need to be captured intact. Every method and every machine runs into the same botanical constraint, and understanding it is the key to understanding why mechanization took so long.

The biology that complicates the harvest

Common milkweed (Asclepias syriaca) is a colonial perennial. It spreads mainly through rhizomes, shallow horizontal underground stems that extend year after year and give rise to many genetically identical shoots: an entire stand is often a single clone, as botanist Craig Holdrege described in detail in his monograph on the species. This shallow root architecture will, as we will see, have direct consequences for mechanical harvesting.

The challenge, however, centres on the fruit. Milkweed produces a follicle, a dry pod that splits along its full length at maturity to release its seeds. Each seed is topped with a silky tuft that acts like a parachute: from the plant's point of view, the floss is a dispersal organ optimized over millions of years to fly off at the first breeze. Harvesting therefore means using the organ against its purpose, capturing it just before it does its job.

Four botanical traits explain most of the difficulty:

  • The pod opens on its own at maturity (dehiscence). Once split, the floss leaves with the slightest wind. The harvest must therefore target the still-closed pod.
  • The pods do not ripen all at once. Flowering happens in tiered umbels along the stem, the lowest opening first; at the optimal moment, a single plant therefore carries pods that are ready, others still too green, and others already open.
  • The fibre is short, smooth, hollow and coated in wax. Remarkable as insulation, it has almost no grip, breaks easily and turns to fine dust as soon as it is handled roughly.
  • The green pod is saturated with water (about 70% moisture) and the whole plant secretes a sticky latex. Harvested pell-mell with leaves and stems, the floss gets contaminated and moulds.

Nature has thus made this floss light, fleeting and fragile, the exact opposite of what farm machinery handles easily.

The field and its insects, including the monarch

A milkweed field is never an inert monoculture: the plant feeds a whole retinue of insects, some harmful to the crop, others entirely dependent on it. On the pest side, the milkweed leaf beetle, a defoliating beetle, can damage the foliage and reduce yield. The latex plays an ambivalent role here: it traps small insects and concentrates toxins (cardenolides) that deter most herbivores, as Holdrege documented in his study of milkweed's companions.

Then there is the species everyone has in mind: the monarch butterfly, whose caterpillar feeds only on milkweed. A common worry is that harvesting the plant endangers the monarch. The calendar rules it out. The pod harvest takes place at the end of the season, once the follicles are ripe, when the last generation of caterpillars has already completed its development and adult monarchs have begun their migration of several thousand kilometres toward the oyamel fir forests of central Mexico. Cutting or combing the stems in the fall therefore happens after the butterfly's cycle on the plant is complete. Better still: growing milkweed grows the habitat the monarch will need the following spring.

What the plant demands of the machine

From this biology follow requirements that any harvester must meet all at once:

  • work within a window of barely two weeks, before dehiscence;
  • pick only the closed pods while leaving stems and leaves in the field (selectivity);
  • handle the pod without bursting the fibre or raising dust;
  • allow fast but gentle drying, from about 70% to 10% moisture, without felting or losing the floss;
  • separate the floss, seed and hull afterward, even though the three are intimately bound together.

No existing farm machine had been designed for this set of constraints. Hence a long series of trials and errors.

Hand picking

Picking by hand satisfies almost every requirement: the operator chooses the closed pod and detaches it without rough handling. It sets the quality benchmark. It remains far too slow to be viable at scale today, however: according to growers, it takes several days for a single field. It sets the quality standard without ever being able to deliver the volume.

The first mechanical prototypes

The industry therefore set out to build the machine. Two major prototypes took on the challenge, each running into a different botanical constraint.

The first, a dedicated harvester designed from scratch, never reached sufficient throughput at consistent quality: between the narrow window, the fragility of the pods and the dust, the useful yield remained too low.

The second, adapted from an imported corn picker, illustrates the trap of repurposing a machine. Corn offers hard, dry, aligned ears; milkweed offers tender, moist pods staggered at varying heights. The result was constant clogging, burst pods and a lack of selectivity, with the machine bringing in too many leaves and too much debris. At Western Illinois University, a specialist put numbers on the dilemma: set for cleanliness, a modified corn picker recovered only about 70% of the pods, blowing the lightest ones out with the debris; set for yield, it filled up with leaves. The two goals remained irreconcilable on that mechanical basis. Several observers also attribute these failures as much to poorly run projects as to the plant's intrinsic difficulty.

The comb and the clogging problem

For lack of a complete machine, a semi-mechanized solution took hold: a comb mounted on the front of a tractor, which strips the pods off as it passes. Throughput climbs to about 2,000 kg per day, a clear step up from hand picking.

The comb suffers from a major flaw, however, directly tied to the rooting described above. Because milkweed spreads through shallow horizontal rhizomes, its stems are only loosely anchored by the end of the season. Instead of detaching only the pods, the comb pulls up whole stems, which pile up in the teeth and clog it. The operator then has to climb down from the tractor frequently to clear it by hand, which cuts into the real throughput and loads the harvest with leaves and stem fragments, and therefore with moisture and latex. The gain in speed is paid for in cleanliness, and thus at the drying stage.

The variable-spacing harvester

The harvester developed by grower Martin Bélanger answers this problem with a different architecture, described in a U.S. patent (US 12,501,859 B2, inventor Martin Bélanger, Dec. 2025). Towed behind the tractor, it picks the pods into a trailer without extracting the fibre. Its heart is a row of helical screws mounted in counter-rotating pairs. Separator cones first comb the stems and guide them into the passages formed between each pair of screws; at the end of each screw, a rotary paddle separator turns upward. Because the pod has a larger diameter than the stem, it is torn off and thrown backward onto a conveyor, while the stem passes through the gap and is carried rearward by the screw.

The spacing between the paddle tips is not fixed: it opens and closes several times per revolution, going from about 0.6 to 2.2 inches depending on the number of paddles. The patent specifies that the rotation speed, the forward speed and this variable spacing are set to detach the pod while avoiding uprooting the stem, precisely the comb's flaw on a plant with shallow rhizomes. The choice to harvest only the pods also stems from an instructive first trial: mounted in front of a combine to harvest and extract the fibre in one pass, it had failed, since threshing calibrated for sturdy grain destroyed the floss. Hence the decision to separate harvesting from extraction. The finished version therefore harvests only the pods, and does so earlier in the season, "when most of the leaves are still present," which protects the integrity of the follicles. According to reports, its efficiency is around 80% at a throughput several times that of the comb.

Hulling and drying

Harvesting is only half the job: the pods then have to be opened and the floss separated without destroying it. The best-documented process comes from Nebraska, where a producer group was already describing its method in 1993: the closed pod is harvested at about 70% moisture, opened in a roller mill, then dried in two stages, first on the farm (to about 30%) and then at the plant (to about 10%), before separation by differences in weight and wind resistance. The material balance is telling: ten parts of pods yield about two parts floss, three parts seed and five parts hulls. The bottleneck is still botanical: the floss felts if it is wetted and agitated, and flies apart into dust if it is handled roughly. This is precisely what used to put buyers off, until a drying process gentle enough to preserve the fibre was developed.

The decisive link in the chain

Harvesting is the bottleneck of the whole industry. Until it is solved, clean, fast and affordable, volume falls short, growers are not paid in proportion to their work, and the fields recede, taking monarch habitat with them. Each iteration of the machine, from the comb to the variable-spacing harvester, moves this link one notch forward.
